title: The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets
harvard_reference: Saito, T. and Rehmsmeier, M. (2015) 'The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets', PLoS ONE, 10(3), e0118432. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0118432.
abstract_summary: The paper argues that ROC plots, although standard for evaluating binary classifiers, can be deceptive on imbalanced datasets where negatives greatly outnumber positives, because specificity (and hence the false positive rate) is intuitively but wrongly interpreted: the same absolute rise in false positives yields only a small change in FPR when negatives are numerous, so the ROC curve looks essentially unchanged. Precision-recall (PRC) plots, which evaluate the fraction of true positives among positive predictions, expose this deterioration and therefore give a more accurate picture of expected classification performance. Using simulated classifiers on balanced (1000:1000) and imbalanced (1000:10000) data, the authors show ROC curves remain identical across the two conditions while PRC curves change; a survey of 58 genome-wide SVM studies found ROC used in 66.7% versus PRC in 6.0%; and a re-analysis of the MiRFinder microRNA study showed tools that appeared adequate under ROC performed near the random baseline under PRC.

claims_supported.claim: ROC plots can be misleadingly optimistic under class imbalance, whereas precision-recall plots reflect performance on the minority class more informatively.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: ROC plots on imbalanced datasets 'can be deceptive with respect to conclusions about the reliability of classification performance, owing to an intuitive but wrong interpretation of specificity', while PRC plots 'can provide the viewer with an accurate prediction of future classification performance due to the fact that they evaluate the fraction of true positives among positive predictions'. Results/simulation section: identical ROC curves for balanced and imbalanced data despite false positives rising from 160 to 1,600 at the same operating point ('The ROC curves fail to explicitly show this performance difference'), whereas only the PRC curves changed. MiRFinder re-analysis: ROC suggested consistent performance across test sets, PRC revealed near-random precision on the second set. The 'minority class' in the paper is the positive class (positives outnumbered by negatives), and precision is defined over positive predictions, so the claim's framing matches the paper.

caveats: The paper's evidence and framing are bioinformatics-specific (genome-wide SVM literature survey, microRNA discovery tools) and its simulations use a strong 1:10 imbalance; the argument is general to any binary classifier but the source itself makes no reference to churn, telecom or the Telco Customer Churn dataset (~26.5% churn, a milder imbalance). The paper compares ROC and PRC plots/curves; it does not evaluate every threshold-based metric, so it should not be cited for claims about F1, cost-sensitive metrics or resampling. Journal name appears as 'PLOS ONE' in Crossref and the publisher's site and as 'PLoS ONE' in Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex; either spelling is acceptable in a reference list.
